title: Counting pairs of letters
objectives: Build the 27 by 27 table of letter pairs from a list of names.

screens.title: The last letter
screens.prose: The file `names.txt` holds 32,033 first names, one a line, in lower case. Its first ten are shown here. Over the whole file, one letter ends more names than any other.
screens.question: Which letter ends the most names?

options.why: You went by the top of the file, where most names end in a. Over all 32,033 names, a comes a close second.
You picked the commonest letter in English text. As a last letter of names, e ends 3,983, fewer than n or a.
Names ending in y stand out, but only 2,007 of them do.

hints.text: The top of the file is not the whole file.
Counted over all 32,033 names, n ends 6,763 and a ends 6,640.

feedback.correct: n: it ends 6,763 names, just ahead of a with 6,640.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The first ten names are not a fair sample of 32,033.

byKey.a: You went by the first ten names. Over the whole file n ends 6,763 names and a 6,640.

explain.text: n ends 6,763 names and a ends 6,640: a close race that the top of the file hides. Only a count over every name settles it. This lesson builds the table that holds such counts for every pair of letters.

screens.title: The pairs of emma
screens.prose: A model of names must learn how a name starts and stops, as well as what follows what. So we write a mark `.` before and after each name: `.emma.`. Slide through its **pairs**: each symbol and the symbol straight after it.
screens.question: How many pairs does emma give, marks included?

hints.text: Step the slider to the end and count the steps.
The last pair is a then the end mark.
start e, e m, m m, m a, a end: 5 pairs.

feedback.correct: 5 pairs: start then e, e m, m m, m a, and a then end.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count every symbol that has a symbol after it.

byKey.no-marks: You counted the pairs inside emma only. The marks add start then e and a then end.
byKey.one-mark: You used one mark. With both, the 6 symbols give 5 pairs.
byKey.symbols: You counted the 6 symbols. The last one starts no pair, so there are 5.

explain.text: The 6 symbols of `.emma.` give 5 pairs, one per letter plus one for the end. The first pair records how emma starts and the last how it stops.

screens.title: The bigram table
screens.prose: Do this for all 32,033 names and add up the counts. The result is the **bigram table** $N$: $N_{ab}$ counts how often symbol $b$ comes straight after $a$, with `.` as the start (a row) and the end (a column). If you built a next-word table in AI basics, this is it with letters for words.

state.caption: Four of the 27 rows and four of the 27 columns. Row: the letter now. Column: the next letter.

screens.question: How many times does n come straight after a?

hints.text: The row is the letter now, the column the letter after it.
This is the row for a.
Row a, column n: 5,438.

feedback.correct: 5,438: a then n is the third most common pair of all.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Go along the row for a to the column for n.

byKey.backwards: You read row n, column a: that is n then a. The pair a then n sits in row a.

explain.text: Row a holds what follows a; its cell under n is 5,438. The cell in row n, column a, 2,977, counts the other order.

screens.title: Three names by hand
screens.prose: Count by hand for three names, each with both marks.
screens.question: Fill in the counts for ava, eve and ana.

hints.text: Each row of the canvas is one name with its marks.
ava and ana both start with a and end with a.
start a 2, a end 2, e v 1; each name gives 4 pairs, so 12.

feedback.correct: start then a 2, a then end 2, e then v 1, and 12 pairs in all.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Walk each name from its start mark to its end mark.

byKey.one-mark: You used one mark per name. Both marks give 4 pairs a name.

explain.text: Each 3-letter name has 5 symbols with its marks, so 4 pairs; three names give 12. ava and ana both open with start then a and close with a then end.

screens.title: Every pair in the file
screens.prose: The 32,033 names hold 196,113 letters between them. Think of `.emma.`: 4 letters and 5 pairs.
screens.question: How many pairs do all 32,033 names give?

hints.text: A name of $L$ letters gives $L + 1$ pairs.
Add one pair per letter and one per name: $196{,}113 + 32{,}033$.

feedback.correct: 228,146: one pair per letter, plus one end pair per name.
feedback.generic: Not quite. A name of $L$ letters gives $L + 1$ pairs with its marks.

byKey.no-end: You counted one pair per letter. Each name also gives a pair into its end mark: add 32,033.
byKey.no-marks: You counted pairs inside names only, $L - 1$ each. The marks add two pairs a name.
byKey.symbols: You counted symbols, $L + 2$ a name. The pairs are one fewer per name.

explain.text: Each name of $L$ letters gives $L + 1$ pairs, so the file gives $196{,}113 + 32{,}033 = 228{,}146$. That is also the sum of all 729 cells of $N$.

screens.title: The start row
screens.prose: Row `.` of the table counts first letters: a starts 4,410 names, k 2,963 and m 2,538.
screens.question: What does the whole start row add up to?

hints.text: How many start marks are there?
One start mark per name.

feedback.correct: 32,033: every name has exactly one first letter.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Each name adds one count to this row.

byKey.whole-table: That is all 729 cells. The start row holds one pair per name.
byKey.letters: That counts every letter. Only the first letter of each name lands in this row.

explain.text: Each name gives exactly one pair out of its start mark, so the row adds to 32,033, the number of names. The end column adds to 32,033 too, one end per name.

screens.title: Cells that stay empty
screens.prose: 102 of the 729 cells are 0: no name in the file has those pairs. A model that gives such a pair chance 0 calls any name holding it impossible; l2 deals with that.

state.caption: Four of the 27 rows and four of the 27 columns. Row: the letter now. Column: the next letter.

screens.question: Which empty cell could never be filled, whatever names we add?

options.why: No name here has q then b, but nothing stops a new name having it.
x then r is absent from this file only. A new name could hold it.
start then q is not empty: 92 names begin with q.

hints.text: Which pair would need a name with no letters?
Look at the top-left cell.
Start then end would be an empty name.

feedback.correct: Start then end: it would need a name with no letters.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Most empty cells are empty by chance; one is empty by construction.

byKey.qb: You picked a pair that is merely unseen. Start then end can never occur, since every name has a letter.

explain.text: Start then end would need a name of no letters, so that cell is 0 by construction. The other 101 empty cells, such as q then b, are only unseen, and a new name could fill them.

screens.question: What can their table never tell us?

options.text: How names start and how they stop
Which letter most often follows a
options.why: Pairs inside a name, such as a then n, are still counted without the marks.

options.text: Nothing: the marks only pad the table
options.why: The mark row and column hold 32,033 first letters and 32,033 last letters.
m then m is a pair inside names, so it is still counted.

hints.text: Which pairs of emma are missing?
start then e and a then end are gone, and so is every first and last letter.

feedback.correct: With no marks, first letters and last letters are never counted.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the 3 pairs here with the 5 of `.emma.`.

byKey.padding: You treated the marks as padding. They hold how every name begins and ends.

explain.text: Without marks emma gives 3 pairs, not 5: start then e and a then end are lost. Every name loses its first and last letter that way, so the table cannot start or stop a name.

screens.title: The rule as a loop
screens.prose:
Number the symbols: `.` is 0 and a to z are 1 to 26. Then the whole table is one loop over the names and their pairs:

```python
for w in words:
    cs = "." + w + "."
    for a, b in zip(cs, cs[1:]):
        N[index[a], index[b]] += 1
```
screens.question: With this numbering, which cell holds n then end?

options.why: That is start then n, the pair read backwards. The row comes first.
You counted a as 0. Here a is 1, so n is 14.
There is no index 27: the end mark shares index 0 with the start.

hints.text: a is 1, so count on to n.
n is 14 and the end mark is 0; the row comes first.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The row is the letter now, and the mark is index 0.

explain.text: n is the 14th letter, so its index is 14, and the end mark is 0. The row is the letter now, so n then end is `N[14, 0]`, which holds 6,763.

screens.prose: Write `bigram_counts(words)`: a 27 by 27 NumPy array of whole-number counts, `.` at index 0 and a to z at 1 to 26. The list `words` (all 32,033 names) is ready, read from `names.txt` in the working directory.
screens.question: Write `bigram_counts`.

widget.how: Python starts the first time you run code here, which takes a few seconds. Submit runs 6 hidden tests: two short planted lists, the whole names file (the total, n then end, start then a), and a name with a repeated pair. `cells(N)` lists the non-zero cells; each answer must equal the expected value exactly.
widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

words = open('names.txt').read().splitlines()


def cells(N):
    # the non-zero cells of a table as (row, column, count)
    return [(int(i), int(j), int(N[i, j])) for i, j in zip(*np.nonzero(N))]

screens.title: Up and down days
screens.prose: A desk records each day's move in a share as up (U) or down (D). Counting (today, tomorrow) pairs gives a 2 by 2 table: the bigram table with two symbols. If you have met Markov chains, it is their transition count. 250 moves give 249 pairs.
screens.question: How many times did a down day follow a down day?

hints.text: All four cells add up to the number of pairs.

feedback.correct: 58: the four cells add to 249 pairs.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The cells add to the number of pairs, 249.

byKey.all-moves: You used 250. Like a name, a run of 250 moves gives one pair fewer: 249.

explain.text: The cells add to the 249 pairs, so D then D is $249 - 70 - 60 - 61 = 58$. With $n$ moves there are $n - 1$ pairs; names get their extra pairs from the marks.

ideas: Wrap each name in a mark, `.emma.`, and count every pair of neighbouring symbols: the bigram table $N$ is 27 by 27, `.` at index 0.
A name of $L$ letters gives $L + 1$ pairs, so 32,033 names give 228,146; the start row and the end column each add to 32,033.
102 cells are 0. Start then end is empty by construction; the rest are only unseen, and a model must not call them impossible.

formula.name: Bigram count
formula.note: With `.` as the start and end mark; the cells add to $\sum_w (|w| + 1)$.
